reference.one_line: 7-year-old boy, day 2 of a severe rhinovirus-triggered asthma attack, improving on salbutamol every 3 hours but still on 0.5 L/min oxygen; preventer under-used, smoke exposure at home.

handoff.summary: Corwin Brannigan-Sefu, 7 years, 24.0 kg, was admitted on 16 Nov with a severe asthma exacerbation needing continuous salbutamol and intravenous magnesium in the emergency department. He is improving: respiratory score 3 of 12, speaking full sentences, peak flow 140 (67% of his best), salbutamol every 3 hours. He still needs 0.5 L/min by nasal cannula after a room-air trial failed at 11:45 while asleep (89%). Two medicine problems are open: the as-needed acetaminophen order is an adult 650 mg dose, and intravenous methylprednisolone was never stopped when oral prednisolone began. Potassium was 3.4 mmol/L at 12:10, recovering without replacement.
to_do: Get methylprednisolone discontinued before the 18:20 dose (prednisolone 24 mg due 20:00)
Get the acetaminophen order corrected to 360 mg (15 mg/kg) before any further dose
Salbutamol 5 mg due 15:00 and 18:00; score before and after
Repeat room-air trial awake this afternoon; if score stays 3 or less, space to every 4 hours this evening by inhaler and spacer
Spacer teaching for mother tonight; finish the action plan and school form
Influenza vaccine before discharge; stop the intravenous fluid as he is drinking freely
if_then: If the respiratory score is 6 or more, then give the extra salbutamol dose; if 7 or more, call the resident
If saturation falls below 92% awake or asleep, then increase the nasal cannula flow and reassess
If he tires, speaks only in words or needs salbutamol more often than hourly, then call the resident urgently and consider a blood gas and intensive care review
If temperature is 38.0 or above, then give acetaminophen 360 mg, not 650 mg

reference.brief_hospital_course: Corwin is a 7-year-old boy with poorly controlled persistent asthma who presented on 16 Nov after three days of a cold and a day of worsening wheeze. At triage his saturation was 88% in room air with a respiratory score of 10 of 12. He received three salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, intravenous methylprednisolone 48 mg, continuous salbutamol from 19:00 to 23:00, magnesium sulfate 1,200 mg and a 480 mL saline bolus. Carbon dioxide fell from 44 to 38 mmHg, chest X-ray showed over-inflation without pneumonia, and the viral panel detected rhinovirus/enterovirus. On the ward salbutamol was spaced from hourly to every 3 hours by the morning of 17 Nov, with one extra dose at 04:10. Oxygen has been weaned from 3 L/min to 0.5 L/min; a room-air trial while asleep at 11:45 failed. Potassium fell to 3.0 mmol/L from salbutamol and rose to 3.4 without replacement. Oral prednisolone 24 mg twice daily started at 09:20, but the intravenous methylprednisolone was not discontinued and a further dose was given at 12:25. One 650 mg dose of acetaminophen, an adult dose, was given for fever at 01:20. Allergy advised daily fluticasone through a spacer, allergen and smoke avoidance, and influenza vaccine before discharge. Inhaler technique was poor (2 of 8 steps); a new spacer was issued and Corwin and his father were taught.

qa.q: What weight is used for dosing, and what should his acetaminophen dose be?
qa.a: 24.0 kg, measured 16 Nov. 15 mg/kg is 360 mg; the active order is 650 mg (27 mg/kg).
evidence: notes: Admission history and physical plan

qa.a: Rhinovirus/enterovirus on the 16 Nov swab; influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 and the rest of the panel were not detected.

qa.q: What is his peak flow compared with his best?
qa.a: 140 L/min at about 12:00, 67% of his personal best of 210; it was 110 (52%) at 08:00.

qa.q: How has the respiratory score changed?
qa.a: 10 of 12 at 18:00 on 16 Nov, 8 at 22:00, 7 on reaching the ward, 5 at 03:00 (6 briefly at 04:00), 4 at 08:00 and 3 since 12:00.
3.9 on arrival, 3.0 at 05:30 on 17 Nov, 3.4 mmol/L at 12:10, with no replacement given.

qa.q: How has his oxygen been weaned?
qa.a: Nebuliser mask at 10 L until 23:00, then nasal cannula 3 L, 2 L from 03:00, 1 L at 08:00 and 0.5 L from 12:00. He has not yet been off oxygen.

qa.q: How long was he on continuous salbutamol?
qa.a: Four hours, 19:00 to 23:00 on 16 Nov, at 12 mg/h.

qa.q: What steroid has he had since the oral steroid was started?
qa.a: Prednisolone 24 mg at 09:20, then methylprednisolone 24 mg intravenous at 12:25, three hours later; another methylprednisolone is due at 18:20 and prednisolone at 20:00.
38.1 at 02:00 on 17 Nov after a peak of 38.4 at 01:00; 37.8 or below since 03:00.

qa.q: Does the low potassium need replacing?
qa.a: No. It is a shift into cells from salbutamol, with steroid and high glucose adding; he is eating, has no losses and it is already rising. Pharmacy would replace only below 2.8 or with weakness or rhythm change, at 12 to 24 mEq by mouth.
evidence: notes: Pharmacy note; Paediatrics progress note

qa.q: Is he ready to go home today?
qa.a: No. The criteria are salbutamol every 4 hours, room air awake and asleep, and teaching done. He is on every 3 hours, on 0.5 L/min after a failed trial, and his mother has not been taught.

qa.q: Was a peak flow measured in the emergency department?
qa.a: None is recorded; the first peak flow in the chart is 110 at 08:00 on 17 Nov.

qa.q: Who entered the acetaminophen 650 mg order?
qa.a: The chart does not say. The order is timed 23:40 on 16 Nov with no prescriber named, and the admission plan written at 22:40 specified 360 mg.

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: The pharmacist reviewed the as-needed orders that afternoon and corrected acetaminophen to 360 mg; no further adult dose was given. The duplicate steroid was missed until evening: methylprednisolone was given at 18:20, and at 20:00 the nurse, with prednisolone in her hand, queried the pair and the resident stopped the intravenous one. Corwin was wide awake and irritable until 02:00 but came to no lasting harm. He managed room air awake on 17 Nov, needed 0.5 L/min overnight, and was off oxygen from 07:30 on 18 Nov. Salbutamol went to every 4 hours by spacer that evening. His mother was taught, the school form was signed, and he had his influenza vaccine before going home on 19 Nov. In the next month he took his preventer daily, had one yellow-zone day with a cold that was managed at home with a same-day clinic visit, and blew 200 at the allergy clinic.

outcomes_30_day.notable: One yellow-zone episode on 2 Dec handled with the action plan and a same-day clinic visit; no missed school after the first week.

portal_messages.subject: Corwin needs another blue inhaler
portal_messages.body: Hi, it's Marit, Corwin's mum. His blue inhaler is nearly empty again, can I get another one sent to the pharmacy? He's been coughing a lot at night and needing it most days, especially after PE. I work nights so his nan gives it to him when I'm not there. Thanks.
ideal_reply_points: A third reliever in eight weeks with night cough means his asthma is not controlled; book a review this week, not just a refill
Ask about the daily preventer and the spacer
When to seek urgent help: reliever not lasting 4 hours, breathless talking, pulling in at the ribs

portal_messages.subject: Re: Corwin needs another blue inhaler
portal_messages.body: Hello Ms Brannigan, as discussed on the phone this morning the refill has been sent to your pharmacy and should be ready after 2 pm. This is his third reliever inhaler in eight weeks, so please book an asthma review with his doctor when you can. The booking line is open 8 to 5 on weekdays.
ideal_reply_points: Should have offered a specific appointment this week rather than leaving booking to the family
Should have asked about preventer use, spacer and night symptoms

portal_messages.subject: Threw up his last steroid dose
portal_messages.body: Corwin had his evening steroid medicine about ten minutes ago and then coughed and was sick, the whole lot came up. It's meant to be his very last dose. Do I give it again or just leave it? He's otherwise fine, no wheeze today, and he did his orange inhaler with the spacer before bed like we were shown.
ideal_reply_points: Vomited within about 15 minutes: repeat the full dose once tonight
If he vomits again, leave it and call in the morning
Praise the daily preventer and spacer use; confirm the review appointment

portal_messages.subject: Cold again, peak flow 150
portal_messages.body: Corwin caught his sister's cold. He coughed in the night and his peak flow this morning was 150, so that's yellow on his plan. I've given the blue inhaler through the spacer like the plan says and he sounds better, he's talking and eating. He's had his orange one every day. Do I keep him off school, and when do I need to bring him in? I'm scared of another night like last time.
ideal_reply_points: She is following the plan correctly; stay in the yellow-zone steps and recheck peak flow after the reliever
Go to the emergency department if peak flow is under 105, the reliever does not last 4 hours, or he is breathless speaking

portal_messages.subject: Re: Cold again, peak flow 150
portal_messages.body: Good morning Marit. You have done exactly the right thing. Keep following the yellow section of his plan and check his peak flow again about 15 minutes after the blue inhaler. We would like to see him today: I have held a 2:30 pm appointment. Keep him home this morning. If his peak flow drops below 105, the blue inhaler stops lasting four hours, or he is too breathless to talk in sentences, go straight to the emergency department.

conversation.setting: Bedside in PD-11, 17 Nov just after the 12:05 nebuliser: respiratory therapist's assessment and inhaler teaching with Corwin and his father

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Right, treatment's done. Corwin, your chest sounds a lot better than this morning. Just a little whistle right at the end of the breath out.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: He's more himself. He's beaten me at cards twice.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Good sign. Corwin, three big blows into this for me, hard and fast, like candles a long way off. ...140. That's your best of the three.

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: Is that good?

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Better than breakfast time, when you blew 110. Your best ever is 210, so you're about two thirds of the way back.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: I thought the doctor said this morning he was off the oxygen. He's still got the prongs in.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: He's needed a little all along. We tried without at quarter to twelve, while he was asleep. Inside ten minutes his oxygen number drifted down to 89, so they went back on the lowest setting, half a litre, and he came back up to 95, 96. He's not quite ready. We'll try again this afternoon when he's awake.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: So he's not coming home today.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Not today. Now, Corwin, this is a pretend inhaler with nothing in it. Show me how you take your puffer at home.

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: Like that.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Thanks. Dad, did you see? Straight in the mouth, no shake, a quick suck and no hold. Most of it lands on the back of his throat. Where's his spacer, the tube?

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: It cracked in the summer. We never replaced it. I didn't think it mattered much, to be honest.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: It matters a lot. Here's a new one with a mouthpiece, his to keep. And the orange inhaler, the preventer: when does he have that?

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: When he's wheezy. A couple of puffs of that as well as the blue.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: That's the thing I most want to change. The orange one doesn't work on the spot. It calms the swelling in his airways slowly, so he needs it every single day, two puffs morning and night, even when he's perfectly well. The blue one is the quick rescue.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: Every day even when he's fine. We'd taken it as a rescue thing.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Lots of families do. OK Corwin, watch me. Shake it. Click it into the spacer. Lips round the mouthpiece. One puff. Slow breath in, like sipping a milkshake. Hold it and count to ten. Then the next puff the same way, one at a time.

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: What if I can't hold it to ten?

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Then just breathe in and out through the spacer six times, nice and normal. And after the orange one, rinse your mouth and spit. Your turn.

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: Click... puff... one, two, three...

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Brilliant, seven out of eight. You missed one thing right at the start.

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: Shake it!

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Shake it. Dad, tell me the steps back.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: Shake, click it in, one puff, slow breath in, hold for ten or do six breaths, second puff the same, rinse after the orange.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Eight out of eight. Now, this sheet is his action plan, like traffic lights. Green is a peak flow above 168. Yellow is 105 to 168. Red is below 105, and that's an emergency.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: And he's 140 now, so that's yellow.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: Exactly, which is why he's still with us. I'll finish writing it up, and there'll be a copy for school.

turns.speaker: Jabari
turns.text: His mum will want all this. She's back this evening.

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: I'll go through it with her tonight. Treatments stay every three hours, next one at three o'clock. If he's still scoring this well this evening, we stretch to every four hours and swap the mask for the inhaler and spacer.

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: No more mask?

turns.speaker: D. Okoro-Fitch
turns.text: If your chest keeps behaving. Deal?

turns.speaker: Corwin
turns.text: Deal.
